implemented: Native SQLite asset HTTP service supports configured Robust listener ports, asset and metadata XML, raw data, store, update dispatch, batch existence, redirects, and remote-delete policy. A native region client and the SQLite service passed live Windows HTTP and restart tests.

Asset redirects preserve the original HTTP dispatcher's handling of a trailing slash and query string. Windows HTTP fixtures verify matching redirect destinations from native and original Robust for full assets, data, and metadata.

The batch asset existence endpoint rejects namespaced array roots and nested elements in string values, ignores namespaced items, and joins adjacent text and CDATA. The same Windows HTTP regression fixture passes against native and original Robust.

Asset uploads reject namespaced roots and invalid XML boolean values, ignore namespaced fields, and accept a leading plus on numeric fields. The XML reader joins text and CDATA in binary, string, numeric, UUID, boolean, date, and flags fields, rejects nested elements in scalar values, and uses the first occurrence of a repeated scalar field. The Windows HTTP fixture compares native and original Robust on uploads and metadata reads.
Asset uploads that supply only a string ID also work with an omitted or empty FullID wrapper. Windows HTTP fixtures verify both runtimes store the bytes under that ID and reject an empty Guid value.

Asset FullID Guid values accept brace-wrapped, parenthesized, and whitespace-padded UUIDs. Native and original Robust pass the same Windows upload and readback checks with the separate string ID omitted.

The grid asset client handles namespaced and split XML boolean values in batch replies. Windows differential HTTP tests verify that native and original clients ignore foreign-namespace items, preserve short replies, and return all false for a foreign root or nested markup in a boolean.

The grid asset client joins text and CDATA in store reply IDs and treats foreign-namespace roots, nested elements, and nil replies as unsuccessful. The Windows HTTP fixture verifies these results against the original connector.

The grid asset client reads split boolean text in update and delete replies and returns false for foreign-namespace roots and nested markup. The Windows HTTP fixture verifies both operations against the original connector.

The grid asset client shares one asynchronous fetch among pending callers for the same asset ID. A Windows fixture against original Robust verifies ordered callback delivery, isolation of callback exceptions, and a fresh fetch after completion.

A Windows HTTP fault fixture verifies that an async grid request can be retried after queue rejection, that two waiting callers share one HTTP 503 and both receive an empty result, and that a later fetch delivers the recovered asset.

The configured grid asset connector requires an AssetService section as in .NET. A Windows differential HTTP fixture verifies the legacy Network asset URL, inherited Basic authentication, UTF-8 and empty credential overrides, and disabling authentication in AssetService.

The native RegionAssetConnector routes stores with foreign asset URLs to the destination Hypergrid asset endpoint. A Windows HTTP fixture verifies UUID rewriting, export restrictions, and that local grid credentials are kept off foreign requests.

The region connector groups Hypergrid existence checks by destination and maps replies to the original request order. Windows differential coverage verifies duplicate, local, and malformed IDs in a mixed batch and checks that foreign batches omit local credentials.

Synchronous region asset reads recognize foreign asset URLs, look up the UUID locally before contacting the remote grid, and store allowed imports locally. A Windows loopback test verifies routing, credential separation, and suppression of local writes for denied imports.

Asynchronous reads of foreign asset URLs use the same import path and pending-request queue as explicit Hypergrid reads. A Windows loopback fixture verifies callback delivery with the original URL and sender, local persistence for allowed reads, and an empty result with no write for denied reads.

The region connector keeps temporary and local assets in the region cache when configured, delegates uncached stores to the backing service, and normalizes null or zero UUID store replies to an empty string. Windows policy tests verify the cache and service call sequence.

Asynchronous region asset reads check memory first and deliver cached results immediately. Windows policy coverage verifies payloadless hits and negative entries deliver an empty result without scheduling work or consulting the backing service.

Asynchronous region reads share a pending fetch by asset ID across both callback APIs, including local cache misses. A Windows regression test verifies both callbacks complete after a single backing-service read.

The native region connector uses separate two-worker queues for local and explicit remote asset reads, with the original queue limits. Windows tests verify routing, shared pending requests, and live HTTP callback completion.
A Windows HTTP contention fixture holds both explicit Hypergrid workers at the remote endpoint and verifies that a local asset read completes before the remote reads are released.

Native region shutdown waits for active asset read workers and delivers empty results to callers whose queued reads were discarded. A Windows regression test verifies exactly-once notification, callback exception isolation, and immediate cancellation after close.

Linux and macOS CI configure the native MariaDB and PostgreSQL asset suites with disposable database servers. macOS fixtures use short private temporary paths for Unix sockets. Runtime evidence from those CI jobs is still pending.

The compatibility workflow builds the original Robust asset host and providers before configuring native tests. Windows CI uses the runner PostgreSQL tools and a checksum-verified MariaDB archive. The workflow requires the managed interoperability suite and both SQL managed comparisons on all three platforms.
The managed Robust SQLite fixture stages the repository's platform-specific native SQLite library in a private directory and adds it to the child process library search path.

Separate public Hypergrid and private asset listeners share SQLite storage. Windows HTTP tests verify independent authentication, import and export policy, the original metadata and existence exceptions, object XML cleanup and creator mapping, and refusal to update or delete through the public service.

The Robust asset connectors register show asset, dump asset, and delete asset in the native console. Windows tests verify metadata and hex output, binary dumps without overwriting existing files, empty and missing assets, and deletion through the console when HTTP deletion is denied.

The original C# grid and Hypergrid connectors pass live Windows HTTP checks against native Robust. AssetMetadata XML round-trips between the .NET serializer and native connector with UTC, local and unspecified timestamps, fractional ticks, custom content type, and SHA1.

A native region and grid asset connector pass live authenticated Windows HTTP tests against the original Robust process and its SQLite asset service. A differential HTTP fixture also verifies preservation of short and empty existence replies and the all-false fallback for malformed, null, and failed responses.

Native PostgreSQL AssetStore supports the original schema through revision 9 and preserves the provider's binary data, update flags, metadata pagination, and refusal to delete. Windows integration uses PostgreSQL 17 to verify fresh and legacy schemas, HTTP operations, restart persistence, and rollback and retry of a failed migration.

The native MySQL asset provider uses the original revision-10 migration, bound binary writes, replacement semantics, and provider-specific metadata and delete behavior. Windows integration with MariaDB verifies fresh and previously populated schemas, HTTP operations, restart persistence, zero-length data, and direct provider operations.

The filesystem asset byte layer supports the original uppercase SHA-256 names, core and OSGrid layouts, spool precedence, legacy raw files, and gzip archives. Windows tests cover concurrent staging, replacing an older archive, corrupt gzip, and empty payloads.

Native Robust loads the original FSAssetConnector module name with a MySQL/MariaDB index and a background spool writer. Windows HTTP integration verifies original metadata schema, access-time throttling, duplicate IDs, secondary-to-primary restart and archival, classic SQL fallback, and metadata deletion with retained payloads.

The filesystem service also uses the original PostgreSQL revision-1 index, which omits names and descriptions and rejects duplicate stores. The public HGFSAssetService module shares the filesystem backend and applies Hypergrid exchange permissions. Windows tests cover OSGrid archive reads, timestamps, duplicate responses, import and export rules, and public delete rejection.

Filesystem console commands show the asset count and stored digest, delete metadata, and import legacy SQL rows. Live MariaDB and PostgreSQL tests cover binary payloads, the original PostgreSQL LIMIT/OFFSET order, and the original force-import duplicate behavior.

Filesystem imports stream one row at a time from MariaDB and PostgreSQL. Windows integration verifies 101 binary rows per provider and confirms an asset delivered before a PostgreSQL query failure remains imported.

The filesystem writer recovers legacy regular-file collisions at archive shard paths. It keeps the original obstruction in a uniquely named sibling and retries the staged asset without blocking other entries. Windows tests cover both archive layouts.

Primary filesystem services honor ShowConsoleStats and log one-minute read totals, average latency, missing metadata and missing payloads. A timed Windows MariaDB fixture verifies the live report. Interrupted console imports log their failure while leaving the server and already imported rows available.
Windows integration verifies native and original .NET Robust sharing MariaDB and PostgreSQL filesystem indexes, spool files, and gzip archives. Each runtime can read payloads archived by the other.

The MariaDB filesystem index preserves the original all-false existence response and zero console count when a database connection cannot open. Windows integration locks and unlocks a dedicated SQL account to verify failure and recovery, and uses a trigger to verify that a rejected delete returns success while retaining the asset.

Native and original Robust acknowledge MariaDB filesystem asset stores when the metadata insert fails. A shared Windows fixture verifies that the payload remains staged, duplicate stores retain the existing payload, and a later retry makes the asset readable.

PostgreSQL filesystem stores read existing metadata before choosing an insert or an access-time update. A Windows fixture runs against native and original Robust and verifies that duplicate stores return the zero UUID and perform both access-time writes when throttling is disabled.

The filesystem service uses SDK-compatible UTF-16 UUID parsing for batch existence checks and provider metadata lookups. A Windows PostgreSQL fixture compares compact and prefix forms and the SSE4.2 low-byte digit behavior against original Robust.

Filesystem fallback reads follow the original object sanitization branches and log promotion from classic storage. Windows MariaDB coverage verifies that a full read can use the fallback when an indexed payload is missing, while raw reads stay empty and the digest console reports the fallback payload.
